images.filename: During the Armory era, the former hydroelectric plant was known as the Rolling Mill. After that, it was the Harpers Ferry Paper (87f69189-1dd8-b71b-0b62-daf002607bd0).jpg
images.caption:
A partly-deteriorated rectangular structure of brick and stone stands at the edge of a shallow waterway.
During the Armory era, the former hydroelectric plant was known as the Rolling Mill. After that, it was the Harpers Ferry Paper Company. The structure, which sits on a foundation that originally dates to the 1834 tilt-hammer shop, symbolizes over 200 years of water-powered industry in Harpers Ferry.
Keywords: cultural landscape; rolling mill; mill; industry; armory; articles

images.caption:
A gate blocks an arched opening through a berm, surrounded by a wall of square stone blocks.
A railroad berm was built in 1892. The rail line that once ran up the Potomac River on the water's edge now crossed the southern end of the Armory Grounds on the berm. Other landscape features are associated with the berm, such as the large stone culvert that was built through the berm to allow water to pass through.
Keywords: culvert; cultural landscape; berm; railroad; tunnel; stone wall; armory; articles

images.caption:
A two-story terra cotta brick house shows signs of damage such as missing window frames and collapsed porch.
Many of the structures that were built by the Standard Lime and Stone Company to house their workers are still standing. The company houses became obsolete in the 1950s, partially due to modern transportation and communication devices that allowed workers to live away from the work site. This structure, part of the Housing Cluster Site A, is composed of terracotta brick and shows signs of structural damage in the form of missing window frames, sashes, and the collapsed porch.
Keywords: cultural landscape; company town; industry; harpers ferry nhp; articles

images.caption: This is the basin at the end of the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal, looking north toward the end of the canal. Guard lock #8 is at the end of the channel on the left. Interstate Highway 68 / US 40 / US 220 runs on that bridge in the background. The Cumberland Masonic Temple and the Emmanuel Episcopal Church are visible to the left, beyond the highway bridge. The Western Maryland Station is just visiable (brick building, center of picture) beyond the highway bridge. Shops at Canal Place are to the right of the basin. Potomac River is to the left, just beyond the flood wall.
